I believe mornings hide tiny gateways. A coffee rim, a pavement crack, a stranger’s smile—each can lead somewhere improbable. This morning, I followed one through a bakery’s back door.

Inside, cinnamon and rain filled the air. Behind the counter, a woman in an apron arranged rolls on an impossibly deep shelf. She looked at me. “You’re late.”

Late for what? I had missed breakfast, perhaps. Before I asked, she placed a pastry in my hands. Folded like a map, its sugar rearranged itself into words: TURN LEFT AT THE MOON.

So I left. I passed a hardware shop where paint cans rolled and three cats shared a newspaper. At Maple Street and Yesterday Avenue, I turned left, though no moon was visible except a crescent reflected in a puddle.

The puddle rippled. The crescent rose. Suddenly I stood on a rooftop garden, surrounded by tomatoes, fireflies, and sleeping cities. A robot sat nearby, polishing a red watering can.

“Did you bring the pastry?” it asked.

I did. We shared it; every bite tasted of childhood summers. The robot explained that the bakery collected lost directions. People forget where they meant to go, and need a reminder delivered in sugar and heat.

When I returned, the woman was gone. My pastry remained, warm in my palm, and its message had changed: KEEP WALKING. THE BEST PLACES HAVE NO ADDRESS.

I did. I still do. On uncertain mornings, I look for another silver rim, another crack, another doorway disguised as something ordinary.

Late for what? I had missed an appointment, perhaps, or breakfast. Before I could ask, she placed a warm pastry in my hands. It was folded like a map, and the sugar on top slowly rearranged itself into words: TURN LEFT AT THE MOON.

“Did you bring the pastry?” it asked.

I did. We split it, and every bite tasted of childhood summers. Then the robot explained that the bakery existed to collect lost directions. People forget where they meant to go, and sometimes they need a reminder delivered in sugar and heat.

When I returned, the woman was gone. My pastry remained, warm in my palm, and its message had changed: KEEP WALKING. THE BEST PLACES HAVE NO ADDRESS.

I did. I still do. And on certain mornings, when the world feels too certain, I look for another silver rim, another crack, another doorway disguised as completely ordinary.

Inside, the air smelled of cinnamon, burnt sugar, and rain. Behind the counter stood a woman in a blue apron, arranging rolls on a shelf that stretched farther than the building had any right to contain. She looked at me and said, “You’re late.”

Late for what? I had missed an appointment, perhaps, or breakfast. Before I could ask, she placed a warm pastry in my hands. It was folded like a map, and the sugar on top slowly rearranged itself into words: TURN LEFT AT THE MOON.

So I left. I passed a hardware shop where paint cans rolled lazily across the floor. I passed three cats sharing a newspaper with obvious disapproval. At the corner of Maple Street and Yesterday Avenue, I turned left, though there was no moon visible except a thin crescent reflected in a puddle.

The puddle rippled. The crescent rose. Suddenly I was standing on a rooftop garden in the middle of the night, surrounded by tomatoes, fireflies, and the distant hum of sleeping cities. A small robot sat beside the tomato plants, polishing a red watering can.

“Did you bring the pastry?” it asked.

I did. We split it, and every bite tasted of childhood summers. Then the robot explained that the bakery existed to collect lost directions. People forget where they meant to go, and sometimes they need a reminder delivered in sugar and heat.

When I returned, the woman was gone. My pastry remained, warm in my palm, and its message had changed: KEEP WALKING. THE BEST PLACES HAVE NO ADDRESS.

I did. I still do. And on certain mornings, when the world feels too certain, I look for another silver rim, another crack, another doorway disguised as completely ordinary.
